footer.blurb: Preserving humanity's wisdom, one life at a time.

hero.tagline: Because No Generation Should Start From Zero.
hero.intro: Every generation inherits land, tools, language and technology from the generation before it. Almost none of us inherit how the people before us actually thought — the judgement earned through failure, the instinct built over decades, the one piece of advice that would have spared us years of learning it the hard way.

problem.heading: Why Narvyaka Exists
paragraphs: Consider what a manual can do, and what it cannot.

A manual can tell you what to do. It cannot tell you what an experienced person does differently — the small warning signs they have learned to notice, and what quietly went wrong before it finally went right.

That second kind of knowledge — judgement, earned the hard way — usually lives in exactly one place: a single human mind. And it usually leaves the world exactly once, on the day that mind stops being reachable.

A nurse's way of sitting with a dying patient, a farmer's read on next week's weather, a teacher's method for reaching the one child everyone else had given up on — all of it gone, the moment the person carrying it is gone.

This is not a rare tragedy. It is the ordinary, daily condition of being human, and it has always been true. What has changed is that, for the first time, we have simple, inexpensive tools — a phone, a recording, a little structure — that can finally change that.

status.heading: Ten records to begin. Every volunteer role open.
status.body: Narvyaka begins deliberately small on records — a handful, preserved carefully, because trust once broken cannot be rebuilt at scale. Volunteering is not capped the same way: the right person is worth more than a quota, and we would rather hear from them now.

link.label: How a Wisdom Record is made

founderLine.quote: My great-grandfather and grandfather passed away before I was old enough to appreciate the questions I should have asked.

slides.quote: Every story kept is a door left open for someone not yet born.
Wisdom is not what we know. It is what we manage to pass on.
A voice recorded once can still be heard a hundred years from now.
The smallest lesson, kept, can outlast the largest fortune, spent.
What we forget to write down, our children learn the hard way instead.
One honest sentence from someone who lived it is worth a shelf of theory.
Memory is fragile. A record is not.
The best inheritance is not what we own — it is what we understood.
Time takes the person. It should not have to take the lesson too.

preserve.heading: A Lifetime of Learning Should Not Disappear in a Moment.
preserve.intro: You are about to make one Wisdom Record. Not your life story — one lesson, the single thing you would want someone to have if you could only pass on one. It has four parts: your voice, a written note, photographs if you want them, and your identity on whatever terms you choose. Nothing here is published automatically.
preserve.testIntro: Before anything is preserved, we ask five simple questions. If the answer is yes to even one, it belongs here.

test.title: Does it save someone time?
test.body: Something that took you years to work out, that another person could have in an hour.

test.title: Does it help someone avoid a mistake?
test.body: A wrong turn you took, described clearly enough that someone else can see it coming.

test.title: Does it reduce suffering, or improve a life?
test.body: Knowledge that would have made a hard thing less hard, had someone known it in time.

test.title: Does it preserve knowledge that would otherwise disappear?
test.body: A craft, a method, a language of work, a way of doing something that fewer people now know.

test.title: Does it help someone live or work better?
test.body: Not motivation. Evidence — that a life or a way of working was possible.

preserve.timeNote: Most records take twenty to forty minutes. Your answers save in this browser as you go, so a lost connection does not cost you your work.

afterSubmit.heading: Thank you. Your record has been received.
afterSubmit.body: It is now with a person, not a system. Nothing is published until a human being has read it and confirmed it is exactly as you meant it. If you gave us a way to reach you, we will write to you before anything goes live.

recordSomeone.heading: Begin With Someone You Know.
recordSomeone.intro: You do not need to find a stranger, wait for training, or become an expert interviewer. The first person worth preserving is very likely already in your life.
who: A former soldier, a farmer, a craftsman
A neighbour who has survived something others are still struggling with

how.title: Ask first, record second.
how.body: Consent comes before the recorder is switched on, and it is theirs to withdraw at any time.

how.title: Let them finish.
how.body: The most useful part of an answer usually comes after the pause you were about to fill.

how.title: Ask for the specific.
how.body: Not "what did you learn" but "what happened, and what did you do". Detail is what makes a record usable.

how.title: Do not correct them.
how.body: Their account is the record. Where something is uncertain, it is marked as their account — not removed.

recordSomeone.consentBody: No record is published without informed, specific consent. The contributor decides, in plain language, what becomes public, what stays private, and what happens to their words — and they can change or withdraw it at any time.
recordSomeone.askHeading: Ask them one question, and listen for the real answer
recordSomeone.askQuestion: What is one thing life taught you that our family — or the world — should never lose?
recordSomeone.askNote: That single conversation, recorded and preserved with care, is a complete act of preservation. It is also, very often, the most meaningful conversation two people will ever have.

volunteer.heading: This Is Not Someone Else's Job.
volunteer.intro: No institution is coming to do this for us. Historians will not interview your grandmother. A university will not sit with your neighbour's father before he passes. That knowledge belongs to ordinary families, workplaces and communities — which means its survival depends on ordinary people. Every role is open, and we would rather hear from you than not.
expectations: None of these roles require credentials. They require patience, curiosity, and enough respect for another person's story to get it right.
New volunteers begin with guidance and light review; independence is earned through reliable work — because accuracy matters exactly as much as good intentions.
Consent is not a checkbox. If someone hesitates, you stop.
You will encounter things you are not sure how to handle. Say so rather than deciding alone.
Do not ask whether you are important enough to help. Ask whose wisdom you can save.
volunteer.formIntro: Applications are read personally — there is no automated stage and no scoring — and everyone who applies gets a reply.

afterSubmit.heading: Thank you — your application is in.
afterSubmit.body: A person will read this, not a filter. We are a small group, so replies take time, and everyone who applies gets one either way.

volunteer.rolesIntro: Every role below is open, and none of them is capped. We would rather hear from one person who is genuinely right for this than fill a quota — so if something here fits you, say so, even if you are not certain.

openings.title: Interviewer
openings.body: Sits with a contributor, works through the eight questions in the protocol, and does not rush them. The single most important role in the project: everything downstream is only as good as the conversation.
asks: Roughly two hours per record, including the arranging and the follow-up.
Comfortable with long silences and with people who wander off the question.
Willing to stop the moment someone hesitates about consent.

openings.title: Writer & archivist
openings.body: Turns each recording into a readable Wisdom Note without changing what was meant, then files it so it can still be found in fifty years. Transcription and translation only — never interpretation.
asks: Roughly two hours per record.
Fastidious about not improving on what someone actually said.
Happy to be pedantic about file names, formats and dates.

openings.title: Translator
openings.body: Carries a record into another language, and marks plainly what does not translate cleanly. A lesson that survives in only one language reaches only the people who already speak it.
asks: Fluent enough in both languages to hear tone, not only meaning.
Willing to leave a word untranslated with a note, rather than approximate it.
Roughly two hours per record.

openings.title: Researcher
openings.body: Checks what can be checked — a date, a place, a public record — and is honest in writing about what cannot. This is what decides whether a record is labelled Documented or Contributor's Account.
asks: Comfortable concluding “this could not be verified” and leaving it there.
Keeps a note of what was checked and where, so the next person can retrace it.
An hour or two per record, often less.

openings.title: Photographer
openings.body: Makes one good photograph of a person, a place, or the thing they made. A portrait gives the voice a face; a workbench gives the lesson somewhere it came from.
asks: A camera you know well — a phone counts.
Asks before photographing anything, every time.
Usually a single visit.

openings.title: Technologist
openings.body: Keeps the archive readable in fifty years — which is mostly a question of formats, backups and discipline rather than clever code.
asks: Opinions about file formats that you can defend.
Prefers boring, well-documented choices over interesting ones.
Occasional work rather than weekly.

openings.title: Community organiser
openings.body: Finds the people whose knowledge would otherwise never reach us — the ones who would never think to volunteer a story about themselves.
asks: Knows a community well enough to be trusted inside it.
Comfortable explaining consent in plain language, more than once.
As much or as little time as you have.

volunteer.commitmentHeading: One volunteer. One contributor. One beginning.
volunteer.commitment: I will help preserve at least one meaningful experience, from one person.
volunteer.commitmentNote: That is the entire founding commitment. Nothing more is required to start, and almost nothing is easier to keep.
pledge: I will not let valuable wisdom disappear without an attempt to preserve it.
I recognise human experience as a shared inheritance.
I will listen before I judge.
I will preserve meaning without deliberately distorting it.
I will respect consent, privacy, and human dignity.
I will value experienced people whether or not they are famous.
I will identify at least one person whose knowledge deserves to survive.
I will help carry useful wisdom forward.

stage1.mission: Preserve at least one meaningful lesson from every willing experienced person.
stage1.vision: A future where human experience can be preserved in its original form, translated across languages, carried across borders, downloaded, shared, and passed from one generation to the next — remaining accessible wherever humanity chooses to live, on Earth or beyond.
stage1.belief: Every expert deserves a successor. Not in the narrow sense of degrees and job titles, but in the sense that actually matters: every person who has spent real years doing something has, in the process, become an expert in something. Expertise earned through living doesn't need a certificate to be real. It needs one thing it rarely gets: a way to reach the next person who needs it.
stage1.name: Narvyaka: one person's knowledge, made known to the world.
stage1.nameBody: The name is not a found word. It was built, deliberately, from Sanskrit roots: nar — a human being — and vyakta — made known, expressed.

stage2.label: The deeper meaning
stage2.heading: Preserve. Connect. Continue.
stage2.intro: The name carries a second meaning, inspired by three figures from the Indian knowledge tradition, each representing one responsibility the archive depends on.

figures.name: Vyasa
figures.body: Remembered as the great compiler of the Vedas and the Mahabharata, Vyasa represents the discipline of gathering knowledge and organising it so it can survive the person who held it. A memory, alone, is fragile. A structured record can endure.

figures.name: Narada
figures.body: The travelling sage — messenger, storyteller, constant mover between people, realms and generations. Narada represents the responsibility to carry wisdom to wherever it is actually needed, rather than letting it sit unused in one place.

figures.name: Kakabhushundi
figures.body: The crow-sage who narrates Rama's story across ages to Garuda. Kakabhushundi represents continuity itself: a voice that speaks once, and keeps teaching long after the moment it was recorded.

stage2.closing: Three responsibilities, one name, one movement.
stage2.note: Narvyaka's name and its three guiding figures come from India. The responsibility they describe, and the invitation to take part in it, belong equally to every country, every culture, and every person willing to preserve one honest lesson.

howItWorks.heading: The Wisdom Record
howItWorks.intro: Each contribution becomes one Wisdom Record — small enough to complete in under an hour, complete enough to genuinely matter. Not your life story. One lesson.

parts.title: 1. The Person's Voice
parts.body: A short recording, in the contributor's own language. Voice carries what text cannot — hesitation, humour, conviction, the exact weight a person gives to the thing that mattered most. It is, and remains, the original source. Everything else — transcript, translation, summary — is a derived version of it, and is always labelled as one.

parts.title: 2. A Clear Wisdom Note
parts.body: The experience, organised around a few honest questions: What happened? What did you do? What worked, and what failed? What would you do differently? What should someone else watch for? Think of it as a method of procedure — for life, not machinery.

parts.title: 3. Four or Five Photographs
parts.body: A portrait. A workplace. A tool, a handwritten note, a meaningful object. Enough to give the voice a face, and the lesson a place it came from.

parts.title: 4. Identity and Context
parts.body: With the contributor's permission: their name, their place, their years of experience. Narvyaka preserves the lesson and the person who earned it — because a lesson without its author quietly becomes advice from nowhere, and loses half its weight.

audioBody: A professionally filmed interview needs a crew, equipment, editing, and a budget most people preserving a lesson today do not have. Waiting for that budget means losing the interviews that couldn't wait.

Audio needs almost none of that. It is affordable, portable, easy to translate — and, most importantly, it keeps the contributor's actual voice, not a professional's rendering of it, at the centre of the record.

Every Wisdom Record can grow later — into an article, a podcast, a documentary, a book. But the source has to be captured first, while the person carrying it is still here to give it. Everything else can wait. This can't.
howItWorks.storageIntro: No single company, website or government will ever be the sole guardian of what Narvyaka preserves. Durability isn't a promise you make once. It's a responsibility you keep showing up for.

storage.title: The original evidence
storage.body: The untouched recording and the original photographs, exactly as they came from the contributor. Nothing is ever edited in place. The recording remains the permanent source of truth.

storage.title: Open, documented formats
storage.body: Plain text and standard images that a person can open in fifty years with no special software — with regular migration as technology changes.

storage.title: Deliberate redundancy
storage.body: Independent backups and trusted institutional partners, so the archive does not depend on any one organisation continuing to exist.

howItWorks.reviewBody: Narvyaka preserves people, not content. No record is published without informed, specific consent — the contributor decides, in plain language, what becomes public, what stays private, and what happens to their words. Private pain is never turned into entertainment, and a record is never selected because it might go viral. Every submission arrives marked 'pending review' and a person reads it before it goes anywhere.
howItWorks.verificationIntro: Records are not silently presented as fact. Each carries one of exactly three labels, and no record is left unmarked.

verification.body: Supported by records, artefacts or independent sources that can be pointed to.
First-hand testimony from the person who was there. Not independently confirmed, and not treated as lesser for it.
Knowledge passed down and reported as it was received, with the chain of telling shown rather than hidden.

howItWorks.sampleIntro: This is the shape of a finished record. Until a real one exists, this is an illustration.
howItWorks.ruleIntro: Every feature proposal must answer three questions. If the answer is not yes to all three, it is set aside.
rules: Will it still be useful fifty years from now?
Does it respect the contributor's ownership and intent?
howItWorks.ruleClosing: Technology may help people find human wisdom. It must never replace the human being at the centre of it.

browse.heading: What has been preserved so far.
browse.emptyBody: Narvyaka begins deliberately small — because trust, once broken, cannot be rebuilt at scale. The first records are being made now. Every one that appears here will have been given deliberately by a person, and read by a person before it went up.
browse.sparseNote: Here is what's here so far.

capsule.audioMissingLabel: No recording available for this record.

founder.heading: A Letter from the Founder
letter: I believe knowledge is humanity's greatest inheritance.

Every generation benefits from the experience of those who came before it. Yet throughout history, countless lessons have disappeared with the people who lived them. Libraries have been destroyed, languages have faded, and generations of practical wisdom have been lost simply because there was no way to preserve and pass it forward.

During my career, working with technology and with experienced professionals from different countries, I saw the same pattern again and again. Documentation may record what was done, but it rarely captures why a decision was made, the lesson learned through failure, or the judgement earned through decades of experience. When people retire or pass away, most of that knowledge disappears with them.

This mission is also personal. My great-grandfather and grandfather passed away before I was old enough to appreciate the questions I should have asked. Today, I would value not only their stories, but their thinking — the principles that guided their decisions, the mistakes that shaped them, and the wisdom they hoped future generations would carry forward.
Narvyaka was created so that this does not have to happen again.

We envision a future where human experience can be preserved in its original form, translated across languages, carried across borders, downloaded, shared, and passed from one generation to the next — remaining accessible wherever humanity chooses to live, on Earth or beyond.
Our purpose is not simply to preserve information. It is to preserve the experience, judgement, and wisdom that make us human.
Because every expert deserves a successor.
Because knowledge should outlive its owner.
Because humanity moves forward when every generation can learn from the one before it.

privacy.heading: Privacy Policy
privacy.placeholderNotice: Placeholder — pending legal review (Master Reference Part XV). The commitments below describe how the system is actually built today, and are what the reviewed policy must not contradict.

sections.title: What we collect
sections.body: Only what you type into a form or record into a microphone, plus the technical minimum needed to serve the page. There is no analytics script, no advertising pixel, no third-party tracker and no cookie used to follow you between sites.

sections.title: What we do with a recording
sections.body: We transcribe it and, where relevant, translate it. That is the whole list. Recordings are not used to train AI models, and will not be, unless a contributor gives separate, explicit, specific consent for that purpose — which we do not currently ask for.

sections.title: Who can see your record
sections.body: Whoever you chose, at the access level you set when you submitted it. The default is that nothing is public. A record can be public, public but anonymous, family-only, restricted to research use, private, preserved but unpublished, published after a date you name, or released only after your death.

sections.title: Changing your mind
sections.body: You can review, correct, restrict or withdraw your record at any time, before or after publication. Withdrawal means removal from the public archive; tell us if you also want the underlying files destroyed, and they will be.

sections.title: Where it is stored
sections.body: On infrastructure operated by Cloudflare. Recordings and images are held in object storage, the structured record in a database, both under our account and neither shared with, sold to, or licensed to anyone.

sections.title: Children and minors
sections.body: This is not a service for children. Contributions are intended for people aged 30 or over; a younger contributor may apply, but their submission is reviewed by a person before anything is accepted.

sections.title: How to reach us
sections.body: Until a permanent address is published, use the contact route given on the volunteer page. A named contact will be added here before any record is made public.

terms.heading: Terms of Use
terms.placeholderNotice: Placeholder — pending legal review (Master Reference Part XV).

sections.title: What Narvyaka is
sections.body: An archive of first-hand accounts, given voluntarily. It is not a professional, medical, legal, financial or safety advice service, and nothing in it should be relied on as one.

sections.title: Accounts are accounts
sections.body: Records are what a person said happened. Each carries a label — Documented, Contributor's Account, or Family Tradition — describing how much independent support it has. Read the label before you rely on the record.

sections.title: Who owns a record
sections.body: The contributor. By submitting, you grant Narvyaka permission to preserve your record and to make it available at the access level you selected, and nothing beyond that. You may withdraw that permission.

sections.title: Using what you find here
sections.body: Read it, learn from it, quote it with attribution. Do not republish records wholesale, scrape the archive, or use it to build a commercial dataset. Records are not licensed for AI training.

sections.title: What we will remove
sections.body: Anything submitted without the subject's consent, anything that identifies a living person who did not agree to be identified, and anything a contributor asks us to remove.

sections.title: Nothing is guaranteed forever
sections.body: We intend this archive to outlast us and we build accordingly. We cannot promise permanence, and we would rather say so than imply otherwise.

consent.heading: Before you begin
consent.intro: Three things, in plain language, before you give us anything.

points.title: Your recording is the original source. Everything else is a derived version.
points.body: The recording remains the permanent source of truth. Anything made from it — a transcript, a translation — is clearly labelled as a derived version and is never mistaken for your own words. A contribution is never quietly turned into commercial data or AI training material: any such use would require a separate, explicit, fully informed decision by you.

points.title: Nothing is published automatically.
points.body: Your record arrives marked 'pending review'. A person reads it. If anything is unclear we come back to you. Only then does it go anywhere — at the access level you choose at the end.

points.title: You stay in control of it.
points.body: You decide, in plain language, what becomes public, what stays private, and what happens to your words. You can review, edit, restrict or withdraw your record at any time, including after it is published.

consent.checkReview: I understand I can review and edit everything before it is published.
consent.checkAge: I am 30 years of age or older.
consent.ageWhy: Narvyaka begins with contributors aged 30 and above, with priority to those 35 and above — not because age determines a person's worth, but because judgement tends to deepen with years lived.
consent.exceptionHeading: Some wisdom cannot be asked to wait for age
consent.exceptionBody: Exceptions are reviewed individually for: young people with exceptional, demonstrable expertise; someone facing a serious or life-limiting illness, because some knowledge cannot wait; and rare cultural, historical or traditional knowledge at real risk of disappearing. Telling us here does not block your submission — it routes it to a person to read.
consent.exceptionPlaceholder: What is it, and why does it need recording now?
consent.consentRequiredError: Please confirm the first statement before continuing.

about.heading: About you
about.intro: This is the identity part of the record. All of it can be withheld, and a withheld identity does not make a record worth less.
about.name: Your name
about.namePlaceholder: As you would like it written
about.anonymous: Keep my name private — publish this as 'Anonymous Contributor'
about.preferredName: Preferred name, or your name in its original script
about.profession: Your work — what you have mainly done
about.professionPlaceholder: e.g. Weaver, civil engineer, farmer, nurse, teacher
about.recordLanguage: The language you want to record this in
about.contactHeading: How we reach you about this record
about.contactBody: Only used to come back to you with questions and to confirm before publishing. Never published, never shared, never added to a mailing list.
about.contactPlaceholder: Optional, but it is how we confirm before publishing

record.heading: The Wisdom Record
record.intro: One question at a time. There are eight, most are short, and any of them can be skipped except the first.

questions.label: What is one experience, lesson, method, mistake, decision, skill, or memory that another person should not have to discover again from nothing?
questions.hint: Take your time with this one. Everything after it is just detail.
questions.placeholder: Say it however it comes out. It does not need to be tidy.

questions.label: What happened? When and where? Who was involved?
questions.hint: Specifics are what make a record usable years from now.
questions.placeholder: The situation, as plainly as you can tell it.

questions.label: What did you do, and why that choice?
questions.hint: Including the reasoning that seemed obvious at the time.

questions.label: What worked, what failed, and what surprised you?
questions.hint: The surprise is often the most valuable part.

questions.label: What should another person remember?
questions.hint: One or two sentences. This is what gets shown on your record's card, so it is worth saying carefully.
questions.placeholder: The one thing you would want them to carry away.

questions.label: In what situations might this not apply?
questions.hint: Knowing the limits of advice is part of the advice.

questions.label: Who else could confirm this, if anyone?
questions.hint: A person, a document, a photograph, a place. This sets how the record is labelled — and 'nobody' is a perfectly good answer.

lineage.heading: Family & learning note
lineage.question: What did the generations before you do or learn, that shaped what you know?
lineage.hint: Parents, grandparents — as much or as little as you know.
lineage.placeholder: Whatever you know, in whatever order it comes.
lineage.disclaimer: We don't ask you to research this. Only what you already know, exactly as you know it — even if it's incomplete or uncertain.

photos.heading: Photographs
photos.intro: Up to five. A face, a place, a tool, a handwritten page. A record with no photographs is a complete record — this step can be skipped entirely.
photos.dropLabel: Drag photographs here, or choose files
photos.dropHint: JPEG, PNG, WebP or HEIC. Up to 300 MB each.
photos.captionPlaceholder: One line, if you want one
photos.maxReached: That is five photographs — the maximum for one record.
photos.tooLarge: That file is over 300 MB. Try a smaller version.
photos.wrongType: That file type isn't supported. Use JPEG, PNG or WebP.

review.heading: Access & review
review.accessHeading: Who should be able to see this?
review.accessIntro: You can change this later. If you are unsure, choose the most private option — nothing is harder to undo than publication.

levels.title: Public
levels.body: Anyone can find and read this record, with your name on it.

levels.title: Public, anonymous
levels.body: Anyone can read it. Your name is replaced with 'Anonymous Contributor'.

levels.title: Family only
levels.body: Kept for the people you name. Not listed publicly.

levels.title: Restricted — research use
levels.body: Available to researchers on request and on record. Not published openly.

levels.title: Private
levels.body: Held for you alone. Nobody else is given access.

levels.title: Preserved, not published
levels.body: Kept safely in the archive with no publication planned. Preservation is the point.

levels.title: Publish after a date
levels.body: Held until a date you name, then published as public.

levels.title: Release after my death
levels.body: Held until we are notified and have confirmed it. Then published as public.

review.previewIntro: Read it once. Anything here can still be changed — use the step numbers at the top to go back.
review.finalNote: Submitting sends this for human review. It does not publish anything.

volunteerForm.contactHint: How we reply. Not published, not shared.
volunteerForm.roles: Which role or roles interest you?

studio.intro: Edit the site by hand — text, colours, fonts, the logo and the photographs. Changes preview instantly and are stored in this browser only. When you are happy, export them and apply them to the code.

options.answer: Narvyaka is a movement to preserve at least one meaningful lesson from every willing experienced person — the judgement earned through decades of living, not facts already written down.

options.label: Register an Account
options.answer: There's no public sign-up. Reading the archive needs no account at all. Volunteer and admin accounts are created only after an application is reviewed and approved — see "Become a Volunteer".

options.label: Contribute Knowledge
options.answer: Preserve one meaningful lesson in under an hour: your voice, a short written note, and a photograph if you want one. Nothing is published without your review.

Every role is open — interviewing, writing and archiving, translating, research, photography, keeping the archive readable, and finding the people whose knowledge would otherwise never reach us. Applications are read personally, one at a time, never scored automatically.
options.label: Become a Volunteer
Upload Documents
options.answer: Photographs and audio are uploaded as part of making a Wisdom Record — there's no separate upload page. Start a record and you'll be asked for them at the right step.

options.label: Knowledge Review Process
options.answer: Every record arrives marked "pending review." A person reads it, confirms anything unclear with the contributor, and only then does it go anywhere — at the access level the contributor chose.

options.label: Manage My Contributions
options.answer: If you have a volunteer or admin account, sign in to see and edit the records you've submitted yourself.

options.label: Support NARVYAKA
options.answer: There's no donation system yet. Right now, the most valuable support is time — preserving one record, or becoming a founding volunteer.

options.label: Contact Us
options.answer: Write to us directly and a person will reply.

options.label: FAQs: Review process
options.answer: Who reads my record? A person, not a filter. Can I withdraw it later? Yes, at any time, before or after publication. How is uncertain information marked? Every record carries one of three honest labels: Documented, Contributor's Account, or Family Tradition — never presented as more certain than it is.
